title: Literary style
seoTitle: Turkish literary style and narrative tenses
intro: Turkish fiction uses the grammar you know in ways conversation rarely does. A story settles on a base tense and leaves it on purpose; long sentences are built from chains of `-(y)Ip` and `-(y)ArAk` and then cut short; older forms such as *gidesim geldi* and *-cAsInA* come back; words move after the verb for rhythm; and the narrator slips into a character's head without a single *diye*. This unit shows how to read those choices, and how to make a few of them yourself.

sections.title: Telling a story: -DI, -mIş and the historical present

blocks.text: A narrative has a base tense, and every move away from it means something. Three bases are common in Turkish prose.

blocks.caption: Base tenses of narration
head: Base
Effect
Where you meet it
rows: the narrator was there, or tells it as if they were; events follow one another
realist novels, memoirs, most modern fiction
distance: the story was heard, not seen
folk tales (*Bir varmış, bir yokmuş*), legends, family history from before the narrator was born, dreamlike passages
the scene happens before the reader's eyes
a climax inside a `-DI` story; sometimes a whole story

blocks.text: Around the base, the other past tenses do their usual work: `-(I)yordu` sets the background and the action that gets interrupted ([B1 unit 1](gp-past-continuous)), `-mIştI` reaches back to an earlier event ([B1 unit 1](gp-pluperfect)), and `-(I)rdI` describes habits ([B1 unit 2](gp-used-to)): *Kasaba sabahları erken uyanırdı.* The aorist without *-DI* gives description a timeless air: *Kasabada herkes herkesi tanır.*

**The historical present.** A story told in `-DI` can switch to the present at its turning point, so that the reader seems to be there: *Kapıyı açtım. Karşımda kim var, biliyor musunuz?* Storytellers often announce the switch with *bir de ne göreyim!* (and what do I see!) or *derken* (and just then). The switch back to `-DI` closes the scene.

**Chains.** One finite verb at the end of a sentence can carry the tense and the person for a whole series of actions joined with `-(y)Ip` ([A2 unit 11](gp-ip)), while `-(y)ArAk` adds how they were done ([B1 unit 7](gp-arak)). Prose builds long sentences this way, and then cuts them with a short one.

items.tr: Kapıyı açtım. Karşımda kim var, biliyor musunuz?
items.seg: Kapı|y|ı aç|tı|m. Karşı|m|da kim var, bil|iyor mu|sunuz?
items.en: I opened the door. And who do you think is standing in front of me?

items.tr: Bir varmış, bir yokmuş; evvel zaman içinde bir padişah varmış.
items.seg: Bir var|mış, bir yok|muş; evvel zaman için|de bir padişah var|mış.
items.en: Once upon a time, long ago, there was a sultan.

items.tr: Annem o yıl İzmir'e taşınmış; ben henüz doğmamışım.
items.seg: Anne|m o yıl İzmir'|e taşın|mış; ben henüz doğ|ma|mış|ım.
items.en: That year, as I was told, my mother moved to Izmir; I hadn't been born yet.

items.tr: Eve döndü, ceketini çıkarıp koltuğa oturdu ve gözlerini kapayarak bir süre öylece kaldı.
items.seg: Ev|e dön|dü, ceket|i|n|i çıkar|ıp koltuğ|a otur|du ve göz|ler|i|n|i kapa|y|arak bir süre öylece kal|dı.
items.en: She came home, took off her jacket and sat down in the armchair, and stayed like that for a while with her eyes closed.

items.tr: Derken kapı çaldı.
items.seg: Derken kapı çal|dı.
items.en: And just then, the doorbell rang.

blocks.text: `-(y)Ip` takes no tense and no person: the final verb gives them to the whole chain. *Çıkarıp oturdu* is two past actions; *dönüpler* or *döndüp* do not exist.
Phrases that move a story on: *derken* (and then, just then), *gel zaman git zaman* (time went by, in tales), *aradan yıllar geçti* (years went by), *bir de baktım ki* ([C1 unit 7](gp-meger)).

sections.title: Older and literary forms: gidesi gelmek, -(y)ArAktAn, -cAsInA

blocks.text: Literature keeps forms that everyday Turkish uses less, or only in fixed phrases. You need to recognize them all, and you can use a few of them yourself.

**To feel like doing: `-(y)AsI` with a possessive.** The `-(y)AsI` form names something wished for or destined. With a possessive and *gelmek*, it says that a wish came over someone: *gidesim geldi* (I felt like going, literally my going came), *ağlayası geldi* (she felt like crying). The person is shown only by the possessive; *gelmek* stays in the third person. It sounds literary, or playful in speech; the neutral way to say it is *gitmek istedim* or *canım gitmek istedi*.

rows.en: he or she felt like going
you felt like going (plural or polite)

blocks.caption: Negative, question and present
head: Form
Example
Meaning
rows: I didn't feel like going at all.
I don't feel like working at all today.
I'm in no mood to work today.

blocks.text: The same form survives in a few fixed words: *olası* (possible, [C1 unit 2](gp-epistemic-adverbs)), and curses such as *kahrolası* (damned, literally may it be ruined). With the dative it makes adverbs of degree: *doyasıya* (to your heart's content, literally until you are full) and *ölesiye* (to death, deadly): *ölesiye yorgun*, dead tired.

**`-(y)ArAktAn`.** In folk songs, folk poetry and some regional speech, `-(y)ArAk` takes an extra *-tAn*: *gülerekten*, *ağlayaraktan*. Standard prose writes `-(y)ArAk`; read the long form as a mark of oral style.

**`-cAsInA`** ([B2 unit 2](gp-cesine)) is at home in literature: *kırarcasına* (as if to break it), *ölürcesine* (as if dying), *delicesine* (madly). The first sentence of *Aşk-ı Memnu* has a boat passing *çarparcasına*, as if about to ram the women's boat (see the [interlude](c2-u02-culture)).

**`idi`, `imiş`, `ise`, `iken` as words.** Older prose, and some writers today, write the copula as a separate word ([A2 unit 2](gp-idi-imis)): *Hava güzel idi* for *güzeldi*, *gelmiş idi* for *gelmişti*, *çocuk iken* for *çocukken*. It slows the sentence down and gives it weight. *Dek* (until) and *evvel* (before, earlier) are the literary partners of *kadar* and *önce*: *sabaha dek*, *evvel zaman içinde*.

items.tr: Birden ağlayası geldi.
items.seg: Birden ağla|y|ası gel|di.
items.en: Suddenly she felt like crying.

items.tr: Bu sabah hiç işe gidesim yoktu.
items.seg: Bu sabah hiç iş|e gid|esi|m yok|tu.
items.en: I was in no mood to go to work this morning.

items.tr: Bütün gece doyasıya konuştuk.
items.seg: Bütün gece doyasıya konuş|tu|k.
items.en: We talked to our heart's content all night.

items.tr: Ölesiye yorgundu, ama uyuyamadı.
items.seg: Ölesiye yorgun|du, ama uyu|y|a|ma|dı.
items.en: She was dead tired, but she couldn't sleep.

items.tr: Çocuk, kapıyı kırarcasına çalıyordu.
items.seg: Çocuk, kapı|y|ı kır|ar|casına çal|ıyor|du.
items.en: The child was knocking at the door as if to break it down.

items.tr: Hava çok güzel idi; deniz sakin idi.
items.en: The weather was very fine; the sea was calm.

blocks.text: Only the possessive changes: *gidesim geldi*, *gidesin geldi*. *Gidesim geldim* is wrong: the wish is what comes, so *gelmek* stays in the third person.
French has the same picture of a wish that comes to you: *gidesim geldi* is close to **l'envie m'a pris de partir**, and *doyasıya* to **tout son soûl**.

In conversation, what follows the verb is known background or an afterthought ([C1 unit 6](gp-postverbal)). Literature uses the same slot for rhythm and emphasis. A subject placed after the verb lingers at the end of the sentence: *Uyuyordu kasaba* holds the image of the town where the voice drops. A time or place after the verb stretches the moment: *Yürüdük, sabaha kadar.* A verb at the very start, in a short sentence, gives suddenness: *Gitti. Dönmedi bir daha.*

**Rhythm.** Prose also works with repetition (*Bekledim, bekledim, bekledim; gelmedi.*), with series of clauses of the same shape separated by semicolons, and with a long sentence whose meaning arrives only with its last word, followed by a short one. Turkish lends itself to the long sentence: everything that describes a noun comes before it ([B1 unit 5](gp-relative-order)), so the reader waits for the head. In this sentence from *Aşk-ı Memnu*, *izdivaç demek* (marriage meant) has to wait for *yalı demekti* (meant a waterside mansion).

blocks.tr: Lâkin Adnan Bey'le izdivaç demek Boğaziçi'nin en büyük yalılarından biri, o önünden geçilirken pencerelerinden avizeleri … fark olunan yalı demekti.
blocks.en: But marriage to Adnan Bey meant one of the largest waterside mansions on the Bosphorus, the mansion whose chandeliers … you glimpsed through its windows as you passed in front of it.
blocks.source: Halit Ziya Uşaklıgil, Aşk-ı Memnu (serialized 1899–1900), chapter 1, as Vikikaynak gives the text, with a list of furnishings left out; translation our own

blocks.text: **Poetry.** Metre and rhyme move words much further. Syllabic metre (*hece ölçüsü*) and the quantitative metre of divan poetry (*aruz*) decide where the stresses fall, and the rhyme word ends the line. To read an older couplet, put it back into prose order. Ziya Paşa's famous line puts the predicate *iştir* in the middle of the possessive phrase *kişinin âyinesi*:

blocks.tr: Âyinesi iştir kişinin lafa bakılmaz / Şahsın görünür rütbe-i aklı eserinde
blocks.en: A person's mirror is their work; words count for nothing. / The rank of a person's mind shows in what they make.
blocks.source: Ziya Paşa, Terkib-i Bend (19th century), in its usual modern spelling; translation our own

blocks.caption: The couplet in prose order
head: Poem
Prose order
Note
rows: an impersonal passive: one doesn't look at words
*rütbe-i akıl* is an izafet ([C1 unit 4](gp-persian-izafet)): the rank of the mind

items.tr: Uyuyordu kasaba; yalnız denizin sesi duyuluyordu.
items.seg: Uyu|yor|du kasaba; yalnız deniz|in ses|i duy|ul|uyor|du.
items.en: The town was asleep; only the sound of the sea could be heard.

items.tr: Gitti. Dönmedi bir daha.
items.seg: Git|ti. Dön|me|di bir daha.
items.en: He left. He never came back.

items.tr: Yürüdük, sabaha kadar.
items.seg: Yürü|dü|k, sabah|a kadar.
items.en: We walked, all the way to morning.

items.tr: Bekledim, bekledim, bekledim; gelmedi.
items.seg: Bekle|di|m, bekle|di|m, bekle|di|m; gel|me|di.

items.note: A correlative ([B2 unit 10](gp-correlatives)) with the verb shared.

blocks.text: Inversion belongs to narration, dialogue and poetry. Reports, essays and formal letters keep the verb at the end ([C1 unit 6](gp-focus-position)).

sections.title: Free indirect speech and the narrator's voice

blocks.text: Fiction has three ways of giving a character's thought. The third, free indirect speech (*serbest dolaylı anlatım*), keeps the narrator's grammar but lets the character's own words through.

blocks.caption: Three ways of telling a thought
head: Way
Example
Whose voice
rows: the character's words in quotation marks, with *diye*
the narrator reports: a noun clause and a verb of thinking
the narrator's third person and past; the character's time words, questions and feelings

blocks.text: **How to recognize it.** The sentence is in the third person and in the past, usually `-(I)yordu` or `-(y)AcAktI` ([B1 unit 2](gp-future-in-past)); yet it keeps the character's own *yarın*, *şimdi* and *artık*, asks the character's questions without *diye* (*Ne yapacaktı şimdi?*), exclaims (*Ne aptallık!*), and uses the particles of speech: *ya*, *işte*, *hani*, *acaba*, *demek*.

**`-mIş` and irony.** A narrator can repeat a character's claim in `-mIş` and keep a wry distance from it ([B1 unit 12](gp-reported-mis)): *Kardeşi yine geç kalmıştı. Çok önemli bir işi varmış!* The exclamation mark tells you the narrator, or the sister, doesn't believe a word.

**The narrator.** Turkish criticism distinguishes the first-person narrator (*ben anlatıcı*), the all-knowing narrator with the omniscient point of view (*hâkim bakış açısı*) and the observer (*gözlemci bakış açısı*); *bilinç akışı* is stream of consciousness. The first Turkish novelists liked a narrator who stops the story to talk to the reader; by the end of the 19th century, Halit Ziya's narrator stays out of sight and slides into his characters' thoughts (see the [interlude](c2-u02-culture)).

items.tr: Ayşe pencereden baktı. Yarın gidiyordu. Bir daha bu sokağı görmeyecekti belki.
items.seg: Ayşe pencere|den bak|tı. Yarın gid|iyor|du. Bir daha bu sokağ|ı gör|me|y|ecek|ti belki.
items.en: Ayşe looked out of the window. She was leaving tomorrow. Perhaps she would never see this street again.

items.tr: Ne yapacaktı şimdi? Kime söyleyecekti?
items.seg: Ne yap|acak|tı şimdi? Kim|e söyle|y|ecek|ti?
items.en: What was she going to do now? Who was she going to tell?

items.tr: Kardeşi yine geç kalmıştı. Çok önemli bir işi varmış!
items.seg: Kardeş|i yine geç kal|mış|tı. Çok önemli bir iş|i var|mış!
items.en: Her brother was late again. He had something very important to do, apparently!

items.tr: Mektubu okudu, bir daha okudu. Demek her şey bitmişti.
items.seg: Mektub|u oku|du, bir daha oku|du. Demek her şey bit|miş|ti.
items.en: She read the letter, and read it again. So it was all over.

items.tr: Hüzünlüydü; gurbette ilk bayramıydı bu.
items.seg: Hüzün|lü|y|dü; gurbet|te ilk bayram|ı|y|dı bu.
items.en: She felt sad: this was her first bayram far from home.

blocks.text: To spot free indirect speech, try adding *diye düşündü* after the sentence. If it fits, you are inside a character's head.
French readers know the device as **style indirect libre**, the voice of Flaubert's Madame Bovary; Turkish builds it the same way, from the narrator's past tense and the character's words.

summary: A story picks a base tense: `-DI` when the narrator was there, `-mIş` for tales and unwitnessed family history, the present for a vivid scene.
The historical present marks a turning point, often after *bir de ne göreyim!* or *derken*.
One finite verb ends a chain of `-(y)Ip`; `-(y)ArAk` adds manner; a short sentence cuts the long one.
*Gidesim geldi*: `-(y)AsI` + possessive + *gelmek* is **I felt like going**; *doyasıya*, *ölesiye*, *kahrolası* keep the same form.
Literary prose may write *idi*, *imiş*, *ise*, *iken* apart, and uses *dek* and *evvel* for *kadar* and *önce*.
After the verb, literature puts what it wants to linger on: *Uyuyordu kasaba.* To read old poetry, put it back in prose order.
Free indirect speech: third person and past, but the character's questions, time words and particles, with no *diye*.
